comparison: Perfect agreement on negative findings (C37-C39, C74). Both evaluations support the lack of CS modulation and spike waveform changes. OpenEval emphasizes the importance for understanding specificity of tDCS effects, while peer reviewers implicitly accept through absence of critique.

Perfect agreement on simultaneous Neuropixels recordings (C67-C71). Both evaluations strongly support this finding. OpenEval emphasizes this as compelling evidence for orientation hypothesis in awake state, while peer reviewers praise the in vivo nature and ability to record during wakefulness as a major strength.

Strong agreement on non-PC modulation findings (C42-C43, C45-C48). Both evaluations support the heterogeneous responses in non-PCs. OpenEval notes higher proportion of modulated neurons (70% vs 46% for PCs) and acknowledges heterogeneity of non-PC types, while peer reviewers praise the wholistic insight across different cell populations.

Strong agreement on electric field measurements (C27-C29, C93-C94). Both evaluations support the field strength measurements and methodology. OpenEval emphasizes statistical fits and validation against literature, while peer reviewers treat measurements as methodologically sound supporting data without challenge.

Strong agreement on PC heterogeneity findings (C31-C32, C34-C36, C40-C41). Both evaluations support the heterogeneous modulation of PC firing rates. OpenEval notes 46% showed significant modulation with appropriate statistics, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm heterogeneous responses as a core result without concerns.

Strong agreement on vermis recordings and regional differences (C49-C54, C58-C61, C55-C57). Both evaluations support the regional comparison showing greater modulation in vermis vs Crus I-II. OpenEval provides specific percentages (62.35% vs 9.42%, p<0.001), while peer reviewers praise systematic investigation across regions as a strength.

Strong agreement on orientation-dependence findings (C62-C66). Both evaluations strongly support this central finding. OpenEval notes juxtacellular labeling and confocal reconstruction of 8 PCs with small sample size caveat, while peer reviewers call it 'elegant and thorough' and potentially explanatory for clinical trial variability.

Agreement on main conclusions (C3-C4, C72-C73, C89-C90). Both evaluations support the central finding that orientation determines tDCS effects. OpenEval emphasizes converging evidence from multiple experiments, while peer reviewers state main conclusions are 'correct' and the study is 'important and compelling.'

Agreement on lower threshold findings (C96-C98). Both evaluations support modulation at 5.9 V/m. OpenEval emphasizes importance for human-relevant field strengths, while peer reviewers implicitly accept validity of observations across stimulation parameters through methodological soundness comment.

Both address regional comparison (C55-C57) showing different PC orientations lead to different modulation. OpenEval provides specific statistical support (Mann-Whitney, p<0.001), while peer reviewers accept regional differences as part of systematic investigation across cerebellar regions.

Partial overlap on mechanistic interpretations and rebound effects (C82). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN noting mechanisms not directly tested, while peer reviewers accept rebound effects as part of findings without challenge. Different levels of scrutiny on mechanistic claims.
